title: Why Do We Keep Playing? | Making Rewards Visible

scenes.title: 끝내려는데, 딱 조금이 남았다
lines: I was about to stop for the day, but I only needed three hundred more gold for a bigger backpack.
Well, I could just earn that little bit more, right? And there goes another day on the farm. I was trying to clock out, but the backpack had other plans.
The first backpack upgrade in Stardew Valley costs two thousand gold. If we imagine having seventeen hundred, an abstract purchase becomes a goal of earning three hundred more.
The important part is not that the reward is enormous. It is knowing what I can get and how close I am to getting it.
Using Stardew Valley and Vampire Survivors, let's explore the game design of keeping rewards in sight.
Is it enough to put a big number on screen? Not quite. First, the player needs to feel why the reward matters.

scenes.title: 갖고 싶어야, 보상이다
lines: Before entering the mine, I packed my tools and some food. But after picking up only a few things, my inventory is full.
Throwing something away feels wasteful, and going home is a long trip. A bigger backpack is no longer just an item. It would solve a problem I am experiencing.
What happens when I see that backpack in the shop now? What used to be just a price tag has become something I actually want.
When designing a game, showing how a reward changes play can be clearer than simply introducing its name.
I can carry more. I can enter a new area. I can tackle a difficult enemy in a different way. The benefit needs to be concrete.
This does not mean endlessly adding artificial inconvenience. It means connecting rewards to things the player already wants to do.

scenes.title: 현재값과 목표를 함께 보여주기
lines: The screen says I have seventeen hundred gold. Is that a lot? It depends on what I compare it with.
Place the two-thousand-gold backpack price beside it, and I immediately see that I need three hundred more. The number now helps me decide what to do next.
Stardew Valley does not keep the backpack price permanently pinned to the screen. You check the goal in the shop, then earn money while playing.
The comparison graphic shown here is our own illustration of that relationship. It is not a progress bar from the actual game.
If a goal is hard to remember, a game could let players pin a desired item and compare their materials with its requirements.
The key question is this: can players understand what they still need without repeatedly digging through menus?

scenes.title: 얻었으면, 달라져야 한다
lines: And finally, I bought the backpack. The original twelve slots expand to twenty-four.
The satisfying part is not just the purchase confirmation. I can now carry the item I was thinking of leaving behind.
I see a goal, work toward it, and gain something that changes what I can do. Connecting those steps makes the reward easier to appreciate.
But what if a spectacular reward animation plays and I cannot tell what improved? It is like being congratulated without getting to open the present.
For a new ability, provide a chance to use it soon. For extra storage, let players see the breathing room. Give them an opportunity to experience the result.
Announcing that a number increased is different from showing why that increase matters. Reward design does not end at the purchase button.

scenes.title: 경험치 바가 다음 선택으로 이어질 때
lines: Now consider Vampire Survivors. Picking up experience gems fills the bar at the top, and leveling up lets you choose an upgrade.
When the bar is almost full, I want to collect a little more experience. Then I wonder what choices will appear and whether I can strengthen my current weapon.
Two things coexist here. Progress toward the next level is visible, but that does not mean every future reward is fully revealed in advance.
So keeping rewards visible does not mean showing every outcome from the very beginning.
You can make progress understandable while leaving room for choice and discovery. Changes in your attacks then give those choices a tangible result.
But a faster-filling bar is not automatically better. If upgrades constantly interrupt play, the rhythm of rewards needs to work with the rhythm of action.

scenes.title: 모든 보상을 화면에 붙일 필요는 없다
lines: Should we put money, experience, materials, and achievements on screen all at once? The goals might be visible, but there might be no room left to see the game.
Experience that changes during combat and a purchase goal set in a shop need to be checked at different moments.
Make frequently needed information immediately readable. Goals checked less often can live in a menu or a list of selected objectives.
Another option is letting players choose the goal they care about now. Instead of giving every reward equal prominence, support their current intention.
The cluttered and simplified interfaces shown here are hypothetical comparisons, not the results of user testing on an actual game.
Visible does not have to mean permanently enormous. Information should be easy to find when needed and help players understand what to do next.

scenes.title: 하나 남았다고, 한 번이면 끝일까?
lines: Here is another question. If I need just one more material, does that mean one more attempt will finish the job?
Not necessarily, if obtaining it depends on chance. One item remaining and the time needed to get it are different things.
This is a hypothetical design example, not a claim about drop rates in a particular game.
If the interface says I am almost there but the goal keeps feeling distant, the expectation may turn into frustration.
Rather than presenting uncertain time as guaranteed, clearly explain the requirements and the actions players can take.
If the goal is too distant, meaningful intermediate changes may help. But a stream of tiny notifications is not the same as meaningful growth.

scenes.title: 보상은 다음 플레이를 위한 약속
lines: Let's bring it together. Keeping rewards visible is not simply putting a giant gift box on screen.
It means connecting three things: how a reward changes play, how close the player is to it, and what they can do next.
Stardew Valley's backpack connects an immediate inconvenience with a concrete purchase goal. Vampire Survivors' experience bar connects short-term progress with choices and growth.
Ask these questions about your own game. Why would I want this reward? Can I tell how much remains? Can I experience the difference after earning it?
And there is an important condition: the play along the way should be enjoyable too. A reward for enduring boredom is not enough to make a good experience.
Instead of a device that prevents players from stopping, think of a reward as a promise of something they want to try next. What could you design from that perspective?
